The effect size is how many standard deviations the means are apart.

An effect size of 1 means that the differences in means are 1 SD apart.
Basically: the SD becomes the new unit

It is a measure of signal strength, so it does not depend on sample size.
To calculate, use:

(mean(x1) - mean(x2)) / sd(x2)

You can get the means and SD from from your summary table like this (make sure to replace the names with the appropriate values)
summary_table[row_number,column_number]

Precision = how narrow a sampling distribution is

The narrower sampling distribution, the higher the precision

SE is the measure of how wide the sampling distribution is, so precision is a measure of how narrow a sampling distribution is
Therefore, precision is the opposite of SE

\(\text{Precision} = \frac{1}{\text{SE}}\)

Today, we are going to look at how working out might affect one’s life. We are going to look at some simulated (and not necessarily, but possibly realistic) data looking at how the number of hours per day somebody spends working out is related to:

how “in shape” people report they feel
resting heart rate (lower is considered more healthy)
productivity, as assessed by a boss or supervisor

If we think about this for a hot minute, it seems reasonable that as people work out more:

they probably feel more in shape
their resting heart rate probably decreases, but only up to a point

initially, heart rate will decrease from unhealthy to healthy levels
once a healthy level is reached, heart rate can’t drop (much) more

their boss has mixed feelings

a little working out probably boosts productivity along with health
a LOT of working out might be viewed as a distraction (“Why is so-and-so at the gym when everybody else is here putting together the big project?”)


There are three data sets. For each, the first variable is average hours per day spent working out. The second variable is, for each data set in turn:

a self-report of how “in shape” each person feels on a scale of 0 to 10
average resting heart rate in beats per minute (bpm)
a “boss-report” productivity rating on a scale of 0 to 10

Memory DeclineRubric (overview)Detailed RubricHints


Dataset · ↗ · ⤓
You work as a statistical consultant for a medical care corporation, and part of your job is to assess patients’ cognitive abilities. Your company is testing out a perceptual task that involves mental rotation, which is the ability to imagine what an object would look like from a different perspective. During the task, the patient is first shown an image of an object and then is asked to determine if a second presented object is the same as the first – merely rotated – or an entirely new object. They complete 100 such trials, 50 where the objects are the same and 50 where they are different. (See the figure below for an example.)
Your company would like to use this task to help diagnose individuals that have undergone cognitive decline. Previous research has established that in healthy individuals, the speed (in milliseconds) at which someone can identify that the second object is the same as the first depends on how much the object has been rotated (measured in degrees); moreover, the relationship is approximately linear. For impaired individuals, the relationship between speed and degree of rotation is approximately flat (i.e., they are unassociated).
Five patients have completed the task described above. Since you are only interested in the cases where the two objects were indeed the same, you have only been given the 50 trials from that condition. Analyzing each patient individually, plot the completion time as a function of the degree of rotation and produce an estimate of the slope (including a 95% confidence interval). Your company would like to know which patients, if any, show evidence of cognitive decline. Produce a short report where you summarize the data, present descriptive results, and draw conclusions about each patient’s cognitive status.

You are interested in people’s ability to ignore irrelevant visual information when under time pressure. To this end, you have run an experiment in which you presented participants with color words written in various ink colors and asked them to report the ink color of each word as quickly as possible. There are two conditions in the experiment: First, a congruent condition in which the word presented is written in the same color ink, for example, the word “red” is written in red (red). Second is the incongruent condition, in which the word presented is written in different colored ink, for example, the word “red” written in blue (red). The stimuli in the study consisted of 4 colors (red, blue, yellow and green) that could be used for both the written words and the ink. Each stimulus was presented 3 times in the congruent condition and 3 times in the incongruent condition (once in each color different from the word). For each presentation of a stimulus, the experimenters recorded the time it took the participant to verbally produce the color of ink that the word was written in. So when presented with the word “red” written in blue ink (red), the participant should say “blue.”
You have hypothesized that it takes additional effort for people to inhibit the irrelevant perceptual information from the obligatory reading of the color word, and therefore that the mean response time in the incongruent condition will be higher than in the congruent condition. You should test this hypothesis using the data provided and produce an appropriate effect size estimate. As usual, make sure you plot and discuss the raw data and relevant data summaries. Dataset for Option 1 · ↗ · ⤓
You are interested in people’s ability to ignore irrelevant visual information when under time pressure. To this end, you have run an experiment in which you presented participants with color words written in various ink colors and asked them to report the ink color of each word as quickly as possible. There are two conditions in the experiment: First, a congruent condition in which the word presented is written in the same color ink, for example, the word “red” is written in red (red). Second is the incongruent condition, in which the word presented is written in different colored ink, for example, the word “red” written in blue (red). The stimuli in the study consisted of 4 colors (red, blue, yellow and green) that could be used for both the written words and the ink. Each stimulus was presented 3 times in the congruent condition and 3 times in the incongruent condition (once in each color different from the word). For each presentation of a stimulus, the experimenters recorded the time it took the participant to verbally produce the color of ink that the word was written in. So when presented with the word “red” written in blue ink (red), the participant should say “blue.”
You have hypothesized that it takes additional effort for people to inhibit the irrelevant perceptual information from the obligatory reading of the color word, and therefore that the mean response time in the incongruent condition will be higher than in the congruent condition. You should test this hypothesis using the data provided and produce an appropriate effect size estimate. As usual, make sure you plot and discuss the raw data and relevant data summaries. Additionally, you have a collaborator who would like to perform a replication of the study. For their power analysis they want to be conservative and use the smallest effect size consistent with your data. Based on the limits of your confidence interval for the effect of congruency on reaction time, make a recommendation for the effect size they should use in their power analysis.

What can residuals tell us about our predicted model?

The estimated “errors” from our predicted model are called residuals.

Since the true errors are random (by definition), if our predicted model is correct, the residuals should also be random.

What is inferential statistics, and how does it differ from descriptive statistics?

Inferential statistics tries to guess the true population based on the sample we have.










You can use the summary table to calculate the confidence interval
The Lower 95% CI is calculated as Mean-1.96*SE
The Upper 95% CI is calculated as Mean+1.96*SE
You can obtain just the CIs by using select(), with the columns you want as input.

summary_table <- summary_table %>% mutate(LowerCI = Mean-1.96*SE, UpperCI = Mean+1.96*SE)
CIs <- summary_table %>% select(sex, LowerCI, UpperCI)
CIs

  <chr>   <dbl>   <dbl>

Plots the mean and the CI for each group
First, we plot the mean using geom_point()
Then we plot CI using geom_errorbar

Memory DeclineRubric (overview)Detailed RubricHints


Dataset · ↗ · ⤓
You work as a statistical consultant for a medical care corporation, and part of your job is to assess patients’ cognitive abilities. Your company is testing out a perceptual task that involves mental rotation, which is the ability to imagine what an object would look like from a different perspective. During the task, the patient is first shown an image of an object and then is asked to determine if a second presented object is the same as the first – merely rotated – or an entirely new object. They complete 100 such trials, 50 where the objects are the same and 50 where they are different. (See the figure below for an example.)
Your company would like to use this task to help diagnose individuals that have undergone cognitive decline. Previous research has established that in healthy individuals, the speed (in milliseconds) at which someone can identify that the second object is the same as the first depends on how much the object has been rotated (measured in degrees); moreover, the relationship is approximately linear. For impaired individuals, the relationship between speed and degree of rotation is approximately flat (i.e., they are unassociated).
Five patients have completed the task described above. Since you are only interested in the cases where the two objects were indeed the same, you have only been given the 50 trials from that condition. Analyzing each patient individually, plot the completion time as a function of the degree of rotation and produce an estimate of the slope (including a 95% confidence interval). Your company would like to know which patients, if any, show evidence of cognitive decline. Produce a short report where you summarize the data, present descriptive results, and draw conclusions about each patient’s cognitive status.
